title: Winning America’s Reindustrialization
gist: BCG estimates US companies will spend roughly $6 trillion domestically between 2025 and 2029 — about a quarter of all US investment and ~3x the prior five years — with ~85% concentrated in data centers/AI compute and electrification. The binding constraint is not capital but capacity: a ~2 million skilled-trade shortfall by 2030, multiyear backlogs in silicon steel and liquid-cooling components, and an aging industrial base running at ~75% utilization with falling asset productivity.

insights.claim: US companies are planning roughly $6 trillion of domestic investment between 2025 and 2029, about one-fourth of all US investment over that period and roughly a threefold increase versus the prior five years.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Sets the size of the addressable industrial capex pool; anchor for sizing backlogs at US industrial, engineering and construction suppliers.
insights.quote: US companies are planning $6 trillion in domestic investments between 2025 and 2029.
insights.locator: For 25 years, US manufacturers had one priority

insights.claim: Two sectors — data centers including AI compute, and electrification including power generation, transmission and distribution — will absorb about 85% of the roughly $6 trillion domestic investment wave.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Concentration this extreme means the capex cycle is really an AI-plus-power trade; diversified industrial exposure is a weaker way to play it than direct grid and data center suppliers.
insights.quote: Just two—data centers (including AI compute) and electrification (including power generation, transmission, and distribution infrastructure)—will make up about 85% of that amount.
insights.locator: Ride the Supercycle of Capital Investment

insights.claim: The bigger profit pool from the buildout sits with companies holding indirect, second-order exposure — suppliers of steel, rare-earth magnets, critical minerals, cooling systems, and power storage, transmission and distribution equipment — rather than with firms selling directly into data center and grid projects.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Suggests hunting for mispriced second-derivative names whose data center/grid exposure is not yet in the narrative, rather than crowded direct plays.
insights.locator: Almost every industrial firm will be impacted

insights.claim: Firms with direct exposure to data center, AI compute and grid projects will win on speed and delivery certainty rather than on price or legacy brand strength and historically acceptable service levels.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Lead time and on-time delivery become the pricing power variable — watch order-to-delivery metrics and expedite premiums as a competitive moat signal.
insights.locator: Map Your Exposure

insights.claim: AI-native new entrants can move from concept to market-ready product faster than large incumbents because AI compresses design, simulation and testing cycles, making speed a greater source of competitive advantage than before.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Product-development cycle time becomes a disruption risk metric for incumbent industrials; slow engineering organizations are structurally short.
insights.locator: Accelerate Product Development

insights.claim: Ford is repurposing its EV battery supply chain to sell battery storage systems to utilities, data centers, and large industrial and commercial customers.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: A template for how stranded EV capacity gets redirected into the grid/data center demand pool — watch other automakers repricing battery assets as energy-storage assets.
insights.locator: Revamp Your Strategy

insights.claim: US manufacturers face a shortfall of approximately 2 million skilled-trade jobs by 2030, putting an estimated $1 trillion of annual economic activity at risk.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Quantifies the ceiling on how fast announced capex can actually be deployed; expect wage inflation in trades and slipping project timelines.
insights.quote: US manufacturers face a talent shortfall of approximately 2 million skilled-trade jobs by 2030, putting an estimated $1 trillion of annual economic activity at risk.
insights.locator: Labor: A Shortage of 2 Million Skilled Tradespeople

insights.claim: The skilled-labor gap is expected to remain acute through 2035 in three specific trades: mechanical and plumbing, electrical, and instrumentation and control workers.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Names the exact chokepoint crafts — staffing, training and electrical contracting businesses touching these trades have a decade-long demand tailwind.
insights.locator: By 2035, the gap will remain acute

insights.claim: Since 1975 the knowledge-work share of US GDP — professional and business services, finance, insurance, information and telecom — has more than doubled while manufacturing's share has roughly halved, structurally hollowing out the trade workforce the buildout now needs.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Explains why the labor bottleneck is structural, not cyclical — it cannot be solved inside a single capex cycle, so expect persistent cost overruns.
insights.locator: A complicating factor is that the US economy

insights.claim: Physical AI and robotics will likely ease manufacturing labor constraints over the long term, but not soon enough for the current buildout, so near-term relief must come from proprietary training, upskilling and automation of the existing workforce.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Implies a timing gap: robotics narratives are real but back-loaded, while training and automation-retrofit vendors monetize immediately.
insights.locator: Over the long term, physical AI and robotics

insights.claim: Toyota's Advanced Manufacturing Technician program, created in 2005, trains multiskilled maintenance technicians in two years, with 95% hired full-time by their sponsoring company and 83% finishing on time.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Benchmark proving in-house pipelines can work at scale; companies without one are more exposed to the trades shortage than peers.
insights.locator: For example, Toyota’s Advanced Manufacturing Technician program

insights.claim: Demand for electric-grade silicon steel, a core material in transformers, is up threefold since 2015, and many critical inputs sitting at the intersection of AI compute and power face multiyear backlogs.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Transformer and electrical-steel producers hold pricing power for years; shortages here are a hard gate on grid and data center commissioning schedules.
insights.quote: demand for electric-grade silicon steel (a core material in transformers) is up threefold since 2015
insights.locator: Supply Chains: Long Lead Times for Key Components

insights.claim: Liquid-cooling systems for data centers depend on highly engineered cold plates, cooling distribution units and manifolds that are mostly produced by a small number of tier-2 suppliers.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: A narrow tier-2 base is where scarcity rents accumulate — identify the private or small-cap manufacturers behind these components before the market prices the chokepoint.
insights.locator: Similarly, the liquid-cooling systems used in data centers

insights.claim: Standardizing product designs is proposed as a deliberate supply chain remedy because reducing complexity attracts new entrants and creates redundant sourcing options.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Standardization erodes incumbent component suppliers' scarcity premiums over time — a medium-term risk to today's bottleneck winners.
insights.locator: To reduce supply chain constraints

insights.claim: Some critical minerals cannot be sourced domestically at all, pushing manufacturers toward allied sourcing, recycling and recovery from existing mineral streams, or moving upstream into their own processing and refining facilities.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Vertical integration upstream is becoming a strategic necessity, not a margin play — watch industrials announcing refining capex as a signal of input desperation.
insights.locator: Other materials, such as some critical minerals

insights.claim: Tesla built a $1 billion lithium refinery in Texas capable of processing roughly 50,000 tons per year of battery-grade lithium hydroxide to bring battery inputs in-house.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Concrete cost benchmark for domestic midstream refining — useful for underwriting competing lithium and critical-minerals processing projects.
insights.locator: For example, Tesla built a $1 billion lithium refinery

themes.theme: Aging asset base and the brownfield-over-greenfield case

insights.claim: US industrial production utilization is around 75%, up from the 2009 low of 68% but still below the pre-2005 average of 81%, so the existing industrial base is both aging and underutilized.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Spare capacity exists on paper but is costly to restart — don't assume headline utilization slack means the buildout can be absorbed without new investment.
insights.locator: Industrial production utilization is currently about 75%

insights.claim: Gross profit per dollar of net property, plant and equipment rose through roughly 2010–2015 as digital tools modernized analog plants, then fell from $0.95 to $0.74 even while gross margins stayed broadly stable, indicating declining asset productivity.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: A decade of asset-productivity decay is the untapped earnings lever — screen industrials on gross profit per dollar of net PP&E to find recovery candidates.
insights.quote: it has since fallen from $0.95 to $0.74, even as gross margins remained broadly stable
insights.locator: Assets are less productive

insights.claim: Since 2009 the Producer Price Index for nonresidential construction has risen about 80% versus roughly 50% for the broader Consumer Price Index, and permitting timelines, litigation risk, regulatory uncertainty and constrained labor and equipment all raise the hurdle rate on new capacity.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Greenfield economics are broken, which redirects spend toward retrofit technology vendors and away from new plant construction volume assumptions.
insights.locator: Building newer and bigger factories may not make economic sense

insights.claim: Modernizing legacy plants with predictive maintenance, digital process control and IoT can lift manufacturing productivity by as much as 60%, and in some cases makes a plant in a high-cost country such as the US competitive with upgraded facilities in lower-cost countries.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Directly challenges the labor-arbitrage assumption behind offshore manufacturing; supports industrial software and automation demand over construction demand.
insights.quote: In some cases, upgrading a plant in a high-cost country such as the US can make it competitive with upgraded facilities in lower-cost countries.
insights.locator: Instead of building new greenfield plants

insights.claim: Schneider Electric retrofitted a 60-year-old plant in Lexington, Kentucky with industrial IoT connectivity, predictive analytics and digital management tools, cutting energy use by 26% and equipment downtime by 20%.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Quantified retrofit ROI benchmark that prospective buyers of industrial digital tools will underwrite against.
insights.locator: For example, Schneider Electric retrofitted a 60-year-old plant

themes.theme: Reshoring, tariffs and geographic concentration risk

insights.claim: The decades-long push to outsource manufacturing to low-cost Asian countries is reversing, pulled back to the US by physical constraints, geopolitical tensions, supply chain risk and evolving tariff policy.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Frames a multi-year structural reallocation of manufacturing footprint spend toward North America.
insights.locator: Localize Value Chains to Prioritize Quality and Speed

insights.claim: Section 232 and related trade actions have made landed-cost calculations more uncertain, and the next phase of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement could reshape which products qualify for preferential treatment.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: USMCA 2.0 renegotiation is a dated catalyst for North American footprint decisions — pressure-test Mexico/Canada exposure before terms land.
insights.locator: Evolving tariff policies are another factor

insights.claim: In a 2022 survey of 183 US manufacturing executives, 73% prioritized resilience and responsiveness, up from 32% in 2019; in a 2025 reshoring survey, 40% said they would pay a 10% to 20% premium to cut delivery times by five weeks.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Buyers are demonstrably willing to pay a double-digit price premium for speed, which supports margin expansion at domestic short-lead-time suppliers.
insights.quote: In a 2025 reshoring survey, 40% said they would pay a 10% to 20% premium to cut delivery times by five weeks.
insights.locator: As a result, US manufacturers want to produce goods closer

insights.claim: More than 90% of leading-edge chips are produced in Taiwan, leaving the AI compute sector on which the entire investment supercycle depends vulnerable to disruption from tensions over the Taiwan Strait.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: The single largest tail risk to the $6T thesis is geopolitical, not economic — hedge Taiwan concentration when sizing AI-linked industrial exposure.
insights.locator: In semiconductors, for example

insights.claim: TSMC is investing roughly $165 billion in the US to anchor advanced chip production and packaging in Arizona.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Concrete scale of the domestic semiconductor buildout; drives multiyear demand for construction, cleanroom, tooling and power suppliers in Arizona.
insights.locator: In response, Taiwan-based chip manufacturer TSMC

insights.claim: Mainland China accounts for roughly 90% of rare-earth magnet production, an input critical to data centers, power equipment, defense systems, EVs and industrial machinery, and MP Materials is building a magnet supply chain outside Mainland China backed by a $500 million commitment from Apple.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Rare-earth magnets are a single-country chokepoint across five end markets; corporate prepayments like Apple's are the funding mechanism to watch for ex-China capacity.
insights.locator: Similarly, Mainland China accounts for roughly 90%

themes.theme: Capital discipline in a higher-rate regime

insights.claim: Capital is abundant but no longer cheap: long-term rates have returned to their historical norm, and about half of large US companies earn less than their cost of capital of roughly 8% to 11%.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Half the large-cap universe destroys value at current hurdle rates — a screen for forced divestitures, breakups and activist targets.
insights.quote: about half of large US companies earn less than their cost of capital (roughly 8% to 11%)
insights.locator: Streamline the Portfolio and Focus on Winning Businesses

insights.claim: Spreading capital across a wide portfolio of businesses is described as a losing strategy that higher rates have made an expensive one, favoring concentration into a smaller number of stronger businesses with clear competitive advantage.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Supports a de-conglomeration trade: expect more spin-offs and asset sales from diversified industrials chasing every pocket of buildout demand.
insights.quote: Spreading capital across a wide portfolio of businesses is a losing strategy, and higher rates makes it an expensive one.
insights.locator: Capital is abundant, but it is no longer cheap

insights.claim: A three-step turnaround sequence — shrink to a smaller core by shedding underperforming units, improve returns from that foundation, then grow by reinvesting into higher-growth areas with digital acceleration — delivered roughly 28% total shareholder return over five years, while companies that tried to grow out of a weak position created little value.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: A testable playbook with a TSR number attached: prefer shrink-then-grow restructurings over growth-first turnaround stories.
insights.locator: Shrink to a smaller core by shedding underperforming business units

insights.claim: Embedding AI and connectivity into industrial products does three things simultaneously: compresses new-product-development cycles, lifts productivity of equipment in the field, and converts an expanding installed base into recurring service, parts and software revenue that is stickier and more insulated from cycles than equipment sales.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: Connectivity is a multiple-expansion story: recurring aftermarket revenue deserves a higher rating than cyclical equipment sales.
insights.locator: Moreover, digital enablement can turbocharge the growth

insights.claim: Caterpillar connects its 1.5 million installed machines to convert its installed base into recurring aftermarket and service revenue.
insights.speaker: Mel Wolfgang
insights.so_what: The reference case for installed-base monetization in heavy equipment; use connected-asset counts as a comparable metric across industrial peers.
insights.locator: For example, Caterpillar connects its 1.5 million installed machines
